question: What is the primary cellular target of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus within the human immune system?
explanation: The virus specifically binds to and infects cells expressing CD4 surface receptors, primarily helper T-cells, slowly depleting their population over time. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h1)

question: A patient is officially classified as having AIDS based on which immunological marker threshold?

options.A: Hemoglobin levels falling under 8 grams per deciliter
options.B: Total white blood cell count exceeding 15,000 cells per microliter
options.C: CD4 count dropping below 200 cells per microliter
options.D: Platelet count decreasing below 50,000 per microliter

explanation: The clinical definition of AIDS includes a CD4 cell count below 200 cells/uL or the development of specific opportunistic conditions regardless of the count. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h1)

question: Which body fluid carries the highest concentration of the virus capable of horizontal transmission?
explanation: Genital secretions and blood contain high viral titers necessary for transmission, unlike casual contact fluids such as sweat or tears. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h2)

question: What describes vertical transmission of the virus?

options.A: Transmission through accidental needle stick injuries in a clinical laboratory setting
options.B: Infection acquired via sharing contaminated drinking vessels in a household
options.C: Spread through airborne droplets generated by coughing or sneezing in closed spaces
options.D: Spread from an infected mother to her child during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding

explanation: Vertical transmission specifically refers to the passing of pathogens from parent to child during the perinatal period. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h2)

question: What is another common clinical term used for the clinical latency stage of the disease?
explanation: During clinical latency, the virus is still active but replicates at low levels, which is why it is also referred to as chronic HIV infection. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h3)

question: Which clinical feature is most characteristic of the acute infection stage following initial exposure?

options.A: Permanent stabilization of CD4 counts above normal levels
options.B: Flu-like symptoms accompanied by a high viral load
options.C: Total absence of any circulating virus in the bloodstream
options.D: Immediate onset of severe opportunistic malignancies

explanation: Acute infection often mimics mononucleosis or influenza, featuring fever, fatigue, and swollen lymph nodes alongside massive viral replication. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h3)

question: Which fungal infection frequently presents as white plaques on the oral mucous membranes of immunocompromised individuals?
explanation: Oral candidiasis, or thrush, is an opportunistic fungal infection that readily overgrows when cellular immunity is depressed. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h4)

question: Why are opportunistic infections dangerous to individuals with advanced immunodeficiency?

options.A: The weakened immune system cannot defend against organisms that are normally harmless to healthy people
options.B: Normal flora inside the human body turns into malignant cancer cells within hours
options.C: The opportunistic organisms produce toxins that immediately destroy all internal organs
options.D: These specific pathogens mutate rapidly to become completely resistant to all known antibiotics

explanation: Opportunistic infections take advantage of a failing immune system, causing severe disease from pathogens that a robust immune system easily controls. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of a viral load test in clinical management?

options.A: To measure the exact amount of active virus circulating in the blood
options.B: To evaluate liver enzyme function before starting medication
options.C: To determine the absolute number of healthy red blood cells
options.D: To screen for the presence of bacterial pneumonia pathogens

explanation: Viral load quantification measures copies of viral RNA per milliliter, guiding clinicians on whether treatment is successfully suppressing replication. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h5)

question: What makes fourth-generation screening assays superior to older antibody-only tests?

options.A: They detect the p24 antigen alongside antibodies, reducing the window period before detection
options.B: They can identify the exact strain of the virus infecting the patient instantly
options.C: They completely eliminate the need for any confirmatory laboratory blood draws
options.D: They rely exclusively on urine samples rather than invasive venipuncture

explanation: By identifying the p24 viral protein before the body generates detectable antibodies, fourth-generation tests catch infections much earlier. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h5)

question: What is the main goal of consistent antiretroviral therapy for an infected individual?

options.A: Completely eradicating all dormant virus from animal reservoirs
options.B: Achieving and maintaining an undetectable viral load
options.C: Permanently curing the underlying genetic mutation
options.D: Preventing the normal production of white blood cells

explanation: While therapy does not cure the infection, it suppresses viral replication to undetectable levels, preserving immune function and preventing transmission. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h6)

question: Why is strict adherence to a daily antiretroviral schedule essential for patients?

options.A: Missing a single dose causes immediate and total permanent blindness
options.B: The medications decompose rapidly in the stomach if taken at irregular hours
options.C: Irregular dosing triggers severe allergic reactions in all patient populations
options.D: Inconsistent medication intake promotes the development of drug-resistant viral strains

explanation: Sub-therapeutic drug levels in the blood allow replicating viruses to mutate and develop resistance to the prescribed medications. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h6)

question: What describes the function of Pre-exposure Prophylaxis?

options.A: Administering a therapeutic vaccine to individuals who already have full-blown AIDS
options.B: Taking antiretroviral medications daily by HIV-negative individuals to prevent infection
options.C: Providing emergency antibiotics to treat acute opportunistic pneumonia infections
options.D: Using topical barrier creams to eliminate bacteria during sexual intercourse

explanation: PrEP is a biomedical prevention strategy where individuals at ongoing risk take medications regularly to block potential viral acquisition. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h7)

question: Which intervention is most appropriate for a healthcare worker following an accidental needle-stick injury from an infected source?

options.A: Taking high-dose vitamins to boost general immune resistance
options.B: Initiating post-exposure prophylaxis medications as soon as possible
options.C: Discontinuing all work duties permanently without further assessment
options.D: Waiting three months before seeking any medical evaluation or blood work

explanation: PEP should be started promptly, ideally within hours of exposure, to reduce the likelihood of systemic viral establishment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h7)
